claims: The Artemis II mission is a 10-day crewed lunar flyby.
The Artemis II mission is scheduled for launch on April 1, 2026.
The Artemis II mission will launch from NASA Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39B.
The Artemis II mission sends four astronauts around the Moon in the Orion spacecraft.
The Artemis II mission returns to Earth via a Pacific Ocean splashdown.
Artemis II launches at 6:35 p.m. EDT on April 1, 2026.
The Space Launch System (SLS) rocket lifts the Artemis II crew into orbit.
On days 1-2 of Artemis II, Orion performs a perigee raise to enter a high-Earth orbit.
After separation from the ICPS upper stage, the Artemis II crew conducts manual close-proximity maneuvering tests with the stage to practice docking, as explained in the CNN Artemis II overview.
Roughly 25.5 hours after Artemis II launch on day 2, the main engine fires for the translunar injection (TLI).
Translunar injection places the Orion spacecraft on a trajectory to the Moon.
On day 6 of Artemis II, Orion enters the Moon's gravitational influence.
On day 6 of Artemis II, Orion loops around the far side of the Moon.
On day 6 of Artemis II, the crew comes within roughly 100 km of the Moon's surface.
On day 10 of Artemis II, the crew module separates.
On day 10 of Artemis II, the crew module re-enters the atmosphere at high speed testing the heat shield.
On day 10 of Artemis II, the crew module lands in the Pacific Ocean.
The Artemis II crew consists of Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch (NASA), and Jeremy Hansen (CSA).
Artemis II is the first crewed mission beyond low-Earth orbit since 1972.
The Artemis II mission duration is approximately 10 days.
